title: He's been blind since birth. He's also saved 13 lives from drowning. October 2, 2026.
excerpt: From a Prime Minister who tied a soldier's resolve to a farmer's harvest, to a blind man who dives into rivers he can't see, October 2's five stories share one thread: every one of them did something that looked impossible from the outside, and simply didn't treat it that way.
bodyHtml:
Every story today involves someone doing what shouldn't have been possible given their starting point - a wartime leader turning a slogan into a food security policy, a scientist from a Gujarat village winning a US agricultural prize, a doctor building a gene therapy for one specific baby in six months, an aircraft industry opening to private manufacturing for the first time, and a blind man who swims and saves lives by feel alone.

October 2, 1904: India's second Prime Minister was born on the same day as Gandhi

Lal Bahadur Shastri was born on October 2, 1904, in Mughalsarai, British India. He became India's second Prime Minister in 1964, and during the 1965 war with Pakistan coined the slogan 'Jai Jawan Jai Kisan' - Hail the Soldier, Hail the Farmer - tying military resolve directly to agricultural self-sufficiency. He led India through the war, including the capture of the strategic Haji Pir pass, before signing the Tashkent Declaration in January 1966.

He grew up in a small Gujarat village. In 2026, a US award named after the father of the Green Revolution went to him

Dr. Karim Maredia was named the 2026 recipient of the Borlaug CAST Communication Award, given by the US Council for Agricultural Science and Technology. He joined Michigan State University in 1989 after a postdoctoral fellowship at CIMMYT in Mexico, and has authored over 130 scholarly publications while securing more than $55 million in competitive research funding. He still serves as Foreign Secretary of India's own National Academy of Agricultural Sciences.

His team built a gene therapy from scratch for one baby. It took six months

Dr. Kiran Musunuru, of Indian origin, co-led the team at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia that designed and delivered the world's first personalized CRISPR gene-editing therapy to a single patient, an infant known as Baby KJ, who had a rare, otherwise fatal metabolic disorder. KJ received his first infusion in early 2025, and within seven weeks could tolerate more dietary protein. Musunuru was named to TIME's 2026 list of the 100 Most Influential People for the breakthrough.

India just rolled out its first privately assembled military aircraft

Tata Advanced Systems reportedly rolled out the first India-assembled C-295 military transport aircraft from its Vadodara facility in May 2026, part of a Rs 21,935 crore deal for 56 aircraft total - 16 delivered from Spain, 40 to be assembled in India. The Vadodara Final Assembly Line, inaugurated in October 2024, is India's first private-sector final assembly line for a military aircraft, with over 13,000 of the aircraft's roughly 14,000 parts now reportedly made in India.

He's been blind since birth. He's also saved 13 lives from drowning

Bhullu Sahni, from Dumduma village in Bihar's Samastipur district, has been visually impaired since birth, but is an expert swimmer taught by his father. He is widely reported to have saved 13 people from drowning in local rivers and ponds, diving in to rescue them by feel and sound alone. Bihar Chief Minister Nitish Kumar publicly honored him, and he's locally known as the 'Jal Yoddha' - the Water Warrior.

Five stories, one thread: a wartime leader who turned a slogan into decades of food policy, a scientist whose small-village origins led to a US agricultural honor, a doctor who compressed years of gene-therapy development into six months for one child, an aircraft industry that just opened its first private assembly line, and a blind man who has pulled 13 people out of water he can't see. None of them waited for permission to do what looked impossible. They just did it.
